title: Vehicle condition and evidence
audience: Car detailers recording the condition of a vehicle before work.
learningOutcomes: Carry out a systematic walk-around and log fragile and defective components before wetting the vehicle.
Agree an exception plan with the owner for any component that could be damaged.
Avoid claiming that a pre-existing defect was caused or repaired by detailing.

instruction.heading: Why the record comes first
instruction.body: Before any water touches the vehicle, its condition needs to be recorded as it is found. The reason is practical. The Auto-Detailing guide notes that most swirls, scratches and water spots are added to paint during washing and drying, so a careless wash can add marks to a finish that already had some. Without a before record, a customer who reports a mark after collection and a detailer who knows the wash was careful have only memory to rely on. A written and photographed record turns that argument into evidence. It also shows where the risk sits before products, tools and water pressure are chosen. This lesson covers how to walk the vehicle, how to log what you find, how to agree a plan for parts that could be damaged, and how to write down what was there without blaming the work for it.

instruction.heading: Walk-around and condition map
instruction.body: Walk the vehicle in a fixed order so nothing is skipped. A practical sequence is paintwork, glass and mirrors, trim and seals, lights, wheels and tyres, the engine bay if it is in scope, and then the interior. Work around the car in one direction and note each defect as you pass it. Look at each panel under a directional light, a torch held low across the surface, because flat light hides fine marks. The Spanish-language manual advises avoiding washing in direct sun and using a light close to the surface to show how badly the surface is damaged. A dark vehicle can hide swirls that appear only under a directional light, so check each panel from more than one angle. Number each defect on a simple condition map and photograph each numbered item, with the owner's permission. Where the clear coat is peeling, flaking or hazy in a patch that does not respond to light cleaning, record it as a suspected clear-coat failure. The show-car sample notes that this kind of breakdown cannot be fixed by abrading the surface, so the record should say that the finish may need specialist assessment.

instruction.heading: Fragile parts and the exception plan
instruction.body: Some components are more likely to be damaged by water, pressure or product than others. Log fragile seals, any repaired panel that is not sealed, loose trim, open ports and vents, modified accessories, exposed aftermarket air filters and interior electronics. A cracked light lens may admit water, so the water risk is recorded even if the lens looks sealed. The Auto-Detailing guide advises covering exposed electrical connections and protecting air intakes with a plastic bag where water could reach them, and avoiding a direct stream on visible electrical parts. Agree an exception plan with the owner before work starts. The plan names the component at risk, what will be done to protect it (covering, masking or leaving that area alone), who agreed, and what happens if the part moves or leaks. Where a component is unstable, add a stop-work note and do not use force on it. The plan belongs in the job file next to the condition map, not in a conversation alone.

instruction.heading: Recording what the work did not cause
instruction.body: Keep two entries in the record: what was there before work, and what the work changed. Never write that detailing caused, repaired or removed a defect unless the record shows it. A pre-existing scratch is recorded as found, with its location and photograph. A step you take, such as removing a bonded residue, is recorded separately, with the product, the area and the result. Avoid wording that suggests the vehicle is now restored or defect-free, because it is not. The record also protects the business where an owner's expectations are too high. If the customer expected a scratch to disappear, the written agreement shows the scope and the limits. Keep the record factual and short, and date it at the point it is made.

procedure: Confirm the owner's permission for photographs and for the condition record before starting.
Walk the vehicle once in a fixed order and note fragile components, defects and modifications on the condition map.
Check each panel under a directional light and from more than one angle. Mark suspected clear-coat failure separately.
Photograph each numbered item in shade, under a directional light.
Agree an exception plan for each at-risk component and record the owner's agreement.
Add a stop-work note for any loose, unstable or leaking component.
Record pre-existing defects separately from any change the work makes, then date and sign the record.

workedExamples.situation: A dark, four-year-old sedan has a repaired front panel that is not sealed, loose rear trim and a cracked headlight lens that may admit water.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you record, and what do you agree with the owner before any water is used?
workedExamples.reasoning: Number each item on the condition map and photograph it in shade under a directional light. Record the unsealed panel and the loose trim as found, with the risk of water entry noted. Record the cracked lens as found and note that water could enter it. Agree with the owner that the lens area is masked or left dry, and that the loose trim is not pressed or worked. Add a stop-work note for the trim. Do not describe the lens as repaired, and do not say the wash caused the crack.

workedExamples.situation: Three weeks after a wash, a customer says a new scratch has appeared on the driver's door. The record from the day shows a light swirl in the same place.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What evidence do you show, and what do you avoid saying?
workedExamples.reasoning: Show the pre-work photograph and the condition map entry for that location. Compare the recorded swirl with the customer's description, and ask for the customer's photograph if one exists. Do not say the wash caused the scratch, and do not say it could not have happened. Record what the file shows, what the customer reports and what remains uncertain. Offer any further assessment as a separate agreement.

equipmentAndPpe: Condition map template, numbered per vehicle.
Camera or phone, used only with the owner's permission.
Directional light, such as a torch held low across the panel.
Exception plan form and stop-work note.
Normal work clothing and closed footwear for walking a vehicle on a wet surface (see “Manual handling, wet floors and site hygiene” for slip controls).

commonErrors.error: Walking around the vehicle after it has been wetted.
commonErrors.prevention: Complete the walk-around before any water is used. If the vehicle is already wet, record what you can see and note the limit.

commonErrors.error: Claiming the work caused or repaired a defect.
commonErrors.prevention: Record pre-existing defects as found, and record work changes in a separate entry.

commonErrors.error: Missing a defect because the light is poor.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the finish under a directional light and from more than one angle.

commonErrors.error: Agreeing to protect a component only in conversation.
commonErrors.prevention: Write the exception plan on the job record and record the owner's agreement.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Photographs of a vehicle can show the owner's property, registration details and personal items. The federal Privacy Act generally does not apply to a business with annual turnover of $3 million or less, but it applies to some small businesses regardless of turnover, including health service providers and businesses that trade in personal information. Take photographs only for the job record, with permission, and store them securely.

Stop work and seek a competent person's view where a component is loose, unstable or leaking. Do not force a loose trim piece or an unsealed panel. Electrical and airbag components are outside this course.

qualityStandard: Condition map complete, with a photograph for each numbered item taken with permission.
Exception plan recorded and agreed for each at-risk component in the case study.
Pre-existing defects recorded separately from any work-caused change, with no claim of cause or repair.
documentationEvidence: Numbered condition map with dated photographs and the owner's permission.
Exception plan with the owner's agreement and any stop-work note.
summary: Walk and record the vehicle before any water is used.
Agree written exceptions for components at risk.
Record defects as found and never claim the work caused or repaired them.

knowledgeChecks.question: When is the vehicle walk-around completed?
options: Before any water is used on the vehicle
After the first rinse, when the paint is visible
Only if the owner asks for a condition report
At the end, once the work is complete

knowledgeChecks.question: A cracked headlight lens may let in water. What is the correct response?
options: Ignore it, because lens faults are outside a wash and are not part of the booking at all
Seal the crack yourself so the job can proceed, since the owner will not notice the sealant after the wash is done
Record it, and agree with the owner how the lens area will be protected before water is used near it
Use more water pressure to clear any moisture from the lens before the owner sees the vehicle again today

knowledgeChecks.question: A customer says a scratch appeared after the wash. Which evidence matters most?
options: The pre-work record showing the condition as found
The detailer's recollection of the job
The customer's verbal description of the scratch
A verbal assurance from the previous owner
